question: A document extraction pipeline reports 97% aggregate accuracy on its validation set. What's the most important reason this number alone is insufficient to justify switching off human review?
options: Aggregate accuracy is an average; it can hide a small document-type segment running at 60% accuracy.
97% accuracy violates the cap on how confident a single number should be.
Validation-set accuracy is always lower than production accuracy in extraction pipelines.
Aggregate accuracy can only be computed once the model is fully fine-tuned.
explanations: Correct — averages hide the worst-performing slice when that slice is small in volume; a tiny segment at 60% disappears into a 97% headline.
There is no such cap; the issue is segment masking, not the magnitude of the number.
There is no general 'validation lower than production' rule; the issue is segment masking inside the aggregate itself.
Aggregate accuracy is a metric over labels; it has nothing to do with fine-tuning, which is also out of scope for this topic.

question: What is stratified random sampling for ongoing error-rate measurement in an extraction pipeline?
options: Sampling extractions uniformly across all incoming documents.
Sampling only the extractions where the model returned the highest confidence.
Partitioning extractions into strata (e.g., document type × field) and sampling within each stratum so every segment gets coverage.
Sampling only the extractions a human reviewer has already flagged as likely wrong.
explanations: That's uniform random sampling; it under-samples rare segments and is exactly what stratified sampling exists to fix.
That biases away from low-confidence cases entirely and isn't 'stratified' — it's threshold-based selection.
Correct — strata mirror the dimensions you care about so rare/high-risk segments get coverage proportional to risk, not raw volume.
That's review-driven; sampling for ongoing measurement must be random within strata, not driven by reviewer suspicion.

question: What does it mean for a model's field-level confidence score to be 'calibrated'?
options: The model has been fine-tuned on the production data distribution.
The confidence score has been normalised to fall between 0 and 1.
The score is computed using log probabilities rather than raw outputs.
Cases where the model reports confidence X are actually correct approximately X% of the time, verified on labelled ground truth.
explanations: Fine-tuning is out of scope; calibration is about the relationship between reported confidence and observed accuracy.
Normalisation is a numeric range, not a statistical-accuracy property; calibration is the latter.
Log-prob computation is an implementation detail; it doesn't make the score calibrated.
Correct — calibration means the score's claimed probability matches its empirical accuracy on labelled validation data, per segment.

question: Before automating a high-accuracy extraction step, what unit should you validate accuracy on?
options: Aggregate accuracy across the entire validation set.
Each (document type, field) cell against a per-cell threshold.
Each individual document, holistically.
Each extraction prompt template revision.
explanations: Aggregate is precisely what the topic warns you not to automate on; it hides segment failure.
Correct — segment-level validation by document type and field is the rule; only cells that pass on their own should be auto-shipped.
Per-document validation isn't the unit — failures concentrate in specific (doc type, field) cells, not in 'whole documents.'
Tracking prompt revisions is an engineering practice, not a segment-accuracy validation unit.

question: Which extraction should be routed to human review?
options: Any extraction the model returns at all, by default.
Only extractions where calibrated confidence is below threshold.
An extraction where calibrated confidence is below threshold OR fields that should reconcile contradict each other.
Only extractions where the document is longer than the model's context window.
explanations: That's 'review everything' — it defeats automation and isn't the routing rule.
Confidence alone is insufficient: a model can be confidently wrong on each individual field of a self-contradictory document.
Correct — the production rule is route on low calibrated confidence OR internal contradiction; auto-ship only when both are clean.
Document length isn't the routing signal; calibrated confidence and contradictions are.

question: Why is uniform random sampling a poor choice for measuring error rates across a multi-document-type extraction pipeline?
options: It produces too much data for a human team to review.
It is mathematically biased because random sampling cannot be unbiased.
It cannot be combined with confidence-based filtering.
It under-samples rare document segments — exactly the segments most likely to be regressing.
explanations: Volume is a budget question, not the structural issue; the structural issue is segment under-coverage.
Uniform random sampling is unbiased in the statistical sense; the issue is power on rare strata, not bias.
It can be combined with confidence filtering; that's not the reason it's inadequate.
Correct — a 2%-volume segment will rarely land in a uniform sample, so you have no power to detect its error rate.

question: A team uses raw model self-reported confidence to decide which extractions to auto-ship. What's the core problem?
options: Raw confidence numbers can't be serialised in JSON.
Self-reported model confidence is uncalibrated until validated against labelled data — '0.95' may correspond to 70% real accuracy on a given segment.
Self-reported model confidence depends on the model temperature setting, which the team cannot control.
Raw confidence is always conservative; using it leads to too much human review.
explanations: Serialisation is irrelevant; the issue is the score's relationship to actual accuracy.
Correct — without calibration on a labelled validation set, the number is decorative; high reported confidence does not mean high accuracy.
Temperature is an implementation detail and not the calibration story.
Raw self-reported confidence is famously over-confident, not over-conservative; the failure mode is the opposite.

question: An extraction pipeline returns four fields, each at high model confidence. The line items sum to $1,200 but the extracted footer total is $1,250. What should the routing layer do?
options: Auto-ship — every individual field has high confidence.
Route to human review — internal contradictions across fields override individual confidence.
Drop the extraction silently and re-run the model.
Ship only the line items and discard the footer total.
explanations: Per-field confidence misses cross-field contradictions; that's exactly the failure mode contradiction-routing exists to catch.
Correct — when fields that should reconcile disagree, the extraction goes to human review regardless of per-field confidence.
Silent retry hides a real ambiguity in the source document; the right move is to put a human on it.
Cherry-picking which fields to ship from a contradictory document silently produces wrong downstream data.

question: Where should confidence calibration be computed?
options: Globally, across all extractions, regardless of document type or field.
Only on the largest document type, because that's where the most data is.
Per (document type, field) cell, because the same raw confidence value can mean different real accuracies in different cells.
Only on the rarest document type, because that's where errors concentrate.
explanations: A global calibration averages over heterogeneous segments — exactly the masking problem aggregate accuracy has.
Calibrating only on the dominant segment ignores the segments most likely to be silently wrong.
Correct — calibration is segment-specific; raw 0.95 may mean 96% in one cell and 64% in another, so calibration must be per-cell.
Rare doc types alone don't give you a calibration story for the rest of the pipeline; calibration must cover every cell you intend to route on.

question: After automating high-confidence extractions, why should you keep an ongoing stratified human-review sample running?
options: To detect production drift — new document templates, OCR changes, vendor format shifts — that can regress specific segments silently.
To re-train the underlying foundation model on the latest data.
To satisfy a regulatory mandate that humans review every extraction.
Because random sampling produces less data than full review.
explanations: Correct — populations shift in production, and stratified sampling is the cheapest way to keep eyes on every segment over time.
Re-training the foundation model is out of scope and not the purpose of ongoing sampling.
There is no such universal mandate; ongoing sampling exists for drift detection, not blanket review.
Sample size is a separate budget concern; the reason to keep sampling is drift detection.

question: An invoice extraction pipeline reports 96.9% aggregate field accuracy. A breakdown by document type shows clean PDF invoices at 99% (95% of volume) and scanned-fax invoices at 60% (5% of volume). The team proposes switching off human review based on the aggregate. What's the right response?
options: Approve — 96.9% comfortably exceeds typical 95% automation thresholds.
Approve, but raise the aggregate threshold to 98% before re-evaluating.
Reject — the aggregate hides the 60%-accurate scanned-fax segment; automate only segments that pass the bar on their own.
Approve only for the scanned-fax segment, since that's where errors concentrate.
explanations: This is the canonical wrong move the topic warns against — automating on the aggregate hides the bad segment.
Tightening the aggregate threshold doesn't fix segment masking; the bad segment still hides at any aggregate level.
Correct — segment-level validation drives the automation decision; the scanned-fax segment stays in human review while clean PDFs auto-ship.
Automating the worst segment is the opposite of the right move; that segment is the one that needs human review.

question: A team's daily volume is 10,000 extractions, including 200 amendments-to-MSA. They sample 1% uniformly for human review (100 docs/day). Why is this insufficient for measuring amendment-segment error rate?
options: Uniform 1% sampling reviews about 2 amendments per day — too few to detect a regression in that segment.
Uniform 1% sampling under-counts the dominant segment, not the rare one.
Uniform sampling is forbidden in production extraction pipelines.
Amendments don't need to be sampled; they're the easy segment.
explanations: Correct — only ~2 amendments per day land in the sample; that's no statistical power to detect even a large regression.
It does the opposite — uniform sampling over-represents dominant segments, not under-counts them.
There's no rule against uniform sampling; the issue is power on rare strata, not legality.
Amendments are typically the harder segment in contracts pipelines and need over-sampling, not less.

question: A model returns raw self-reported confidence 0.95 on amendment effective-date extractions. A labelled validation check shows that 0.95-raw cases are right only 64% of the time on this segment. What does the routing layer do?
options: Build a calibration map for the (amendment, effective-date) cell and route on the calibrated probability, not the raw 0.95.
Trust the raw 0.95 — model self-reports are the canonical confidence source.
Assume the validation set is wrong and ignore the discrepancy.
Switch to a different model with better natural confidence calibration.
explanations: Correct — calibration is exactly the fix when raw confidence diverges from real accuracy; route on the calibrated number, per cell.
Raw self-reported confidence is uncalibrated by default; trusting it is the failure mode the topic warns against.
The validation set is the ground truth you calibrate against; ignoring it means you have no evidence at all.
Switching models is over-engineered when the existing model can be calibrated; you'd still need to calibrate the new model anyway.

question: A team is choosing between two routing rules. Rule A: route to human if calibrated confidence < 0.95. Rule B: route to human if calibrated confidence < 0.95 OR there's an internal contradiction across fields that should reconcile. Which is correct, and why?
options: Rule A — a model that's confident on every field is by definition not contradicting itself.
Rule B — a model can be confidently wrong on each individual field of a self-contradictory document; the OR catches that case.
Rule A — adding contradictions to the rule increases the human queue without benefit.
Rule B — but only because Rule A produces too much auto-shipped volume in absolute numbers.
explanations: Per-field confidence and cross-field contradictions are different signals; high per-field confidence does not preclude global inconsistency.
Correct — contradictions are an independent signal; auto-shipping only when both signals are clean is the production rule.
Contradictions catch a real failure mode (high-confidence-but-self-inconsistent extractions); they are the benefit, not noise.
The justification isn't volume — it's that contradictions catch a failure mode confidence alone misses.

question: A 5-doc-type × 22-field pipeline reports 98% aggregate accuracy. A per-cell breakdown reveals that 14 cells are above 99%, 2 cells are at 92–94%, and 1 cell is at 71%. What is the right rollout?
options: Auto-ship every cell since the aggregate clears 95%.
Auto-ship none until every cell is at 99%.
Auto-ship the 14 strong cells; leave the 3 weaker cells in human review.
Auto-ship the strongest 2 cells only and review the rest.
explanations: That's automating on the aggregate — the canonical wrong move.
Holding everything until 100% of cells hit 99% blocks legitimate automation; mixed-mode rollout exists for exactly this reason.
Correct — segment-level rollout: cells that pass their threshold auto-ship; cells that fail stay reviewed.
Over-conservative; many cells comfortably pass the bar and should auto-ship to free up reviewer capacity for the failing cells.

question: A team allocates its 100-doc-per-day human review budget by document-type strata: 30 to amendments (200 daily volume), 40 to MSAs (1,000 volume), 30 to invoices (8,800 volume). Critics call this 'unfair' because invoices are the majority. Is the allocation defensible?
options: No — sampling should be proportional to volume so the dominant segment gets the most review.
No — random sampling cannot be allocated by hand without breaking statistical validity.
Yes — but only if each stratum is sampled with the same percentage.
Yes — stratified sampling allocates by risk, not by raw volume; rare/high-risk segments are deliberately over-sampled.
explanations: Volume-proportional allocation is uniform sampling in disguise; it leaves rare segments under-powered.
You can absolutely allocate sample budget by stratum and remain randomly sampled within each stratum; that's the definition of stratified random sampling.
Equal-percentage sampling is just uniform sampling; equal-power-per-stratum is what stratification provides.
Correct — over-sampling rare/high-risk strata is the whole point of stratification; you trade volume coverage for statistical power on segments that matter.

question: A pipeline auto-ships fields when raw model confidence ≥ 0.9, with no segment-level validation. Production complaints reveal that amendments-to-MSA auto-ship at high error rates. What's the smallest-scope correct fix?
options: Switch to a smaller, more conservative model across the entire pipeline.
Calibrate confidence per (document type, field) cell on labelled data; set per-cell thresholds; only auto-ship cells that pass.
Lower the global confidence threshold from 0.9 to 0.8 to widen human review.
Disable auto-ship entirely and have humans review every extraction.
explanations: Model swap is over-scope; the issue is calibration and segment-level thresholds, not model capacity.
Correct — per-cell calibration plus per-cell thresholds is the targeted fix that addresses the actual failure mode.
A lower global threshold floods human review with cases that are fine in other segments while still mis-routing the broken segment.
Defeats the whole point of automation; the right answer is segment-aware automation, not blanket review.

question: After three weeks of stable production, the stratified review sample shows that NDA effective-date accuracy has dropped from 99% to 88%. Other segments are stable. What is the most likely diagnosis to investigate first?
options: The aggregate accuracy metric has drifted upward.
Production drift in the NDA segment specifically — a new template, OCR change, or vendor format shift.
The model's underlying training data has degraded.
Random noise in the stratified sample; ignore it for now.
explanations: Aggregate accuracy is exactly what stratified-by-segment monitoring is meant to bypass; aggregate movement isn't the diagnostic.
Correct — segment-specific regression after stable performance is the textbook signal of a localised production drift, which is why ongoing stratified sampling exists.
Foundation-model training is static; the model didn't get worse on its own — the input distribution shifted.
An 11-point drop in a stratified sample is a strong signal, not noise; ignoring it defeats the purpose of monitoring.

question: A reviewer asks: 'We have a labelled validation set, model self-reported confidence per field, and per-cell accuracy numbers. What's the calibration step?'
options: Bucket validation cases by reported confidence per (doc type, field), compute observed accuracy in each bucket, and build a map from raw to calibrated probability per cell.
Average the model's confidence with the per-cell accuracy to produce a blended score.
Discard the model's confidence and use per-cell accuracy directly as the routing signal.
Use the per-cell accuracy as a hard threshold and ignore confidence entirely.
explanations: Correct — calibration buckets per cell, computes empirical accuracy per bucket, and maps raw → calibrated; that map drives routing.
Averaging two non-comparable quantities doesn't produce a calibrated probability; it produces nonsense.
Per-cell accuracy is a single number per cell; you lose the ability to differentiate within-cell which extractions are riskier.
Ignoring confidence flattens routing — every extraction in a cell would be treated identically, which defeats per-extraction routing entirely.

question: An extraction returns four fields, all at calibrated confidence 0.99, but two of those fields are mutually inconsistent (extracted parties don't match the signature block). The team's rule auto-ships when calibrated confidence ≥ 0.95. What ships?
options: All four fields auto-ship — confidence comfortably exceeds the threshold.
Nothing auto-ships — the contradiction routes the entire extraction to human review.
The two consistent fields auto-ship; the two inconsistent ones go to review.
All four fields auto-ship with a contradiction warning attached for downstream consumers.
explanations: Confidence-only routing misses contradictions; that's the failure mode the OR-rule exists to catch.
Correct — when fields that should reconcile contradict each other, the extraction goes to human review regardless of confidence.
Cherry-picking which fields to ship from a contradictory extraction silently produces inconsistent downstream data.
Pushing contradictions downstream as 'warnings' delegates the problem to consumers who lack reviewer context to resolve it.

question: A team operates one global confidence threshold of 0.95 across all (doc type, field) cells. An audit shows two failure modes: (a) NDA cells at 0.95 are right 99% of the time, so review is wasted; (b) amendment cells at 0.95 are right 70% of the time, so wrong extractions auto-ship. What's the structural fix?
options: Raise the global threshold to 0.99 to cover the worst cell.
Lower the global threshold to 0.85 to catch more amendment errors.
Drop the global threshold; calibrate per cell and set per-cell thresholds.
Use the global threshold but add contradiction routing on top.
explanations: Raising the global threshold over-reviews safe cells like NDA without fixing the calibration mismatch on amendments.
Lowering the global threshold floods reviewers on safe cells while still mis-routing the unsafe ones.
Correct — calibration is segment-specific; one global threshold is structurally wrong, and per-cell thresholds are the fix.
Contradiction routing is an additional layer, not a substitute for per-cell calibrated thresholds.

question: A pipeline ships extractions to a downstream system. After automation, what's the role of the ongoing stratified human review sample?
options: To act as the primary auto-ship gate for every extraction.
To detect production drift — new templates, OCR shifts, vendor changes — before they regress segments silently.
To replace the labelled validation set used for calibration.
To re-train the model in real time.
explanations: Auto-ship runs on calibrated confidence + contradictions; the sample is for monitoring, not gating.
Correct — populations shift over time, and stratified sampling keeps eyes on every segment so drift surfaces in days, not months.
The labelled validation set is built and maintained separately; the stratified sample is for ongoing monitoring, not calibration replacement.
Real-time re-training is out of scope and not the role of ongoing review.

question: A reviewer-time budget allows 100 reviews/day. Which of these allocations represents stratified random sampling of 10,000 daily extractions across 4 doc types (NDAs 6,000, MSAs 2,000, invoices 1,800, amendments 200)?
options: 100 reviews allocated uniformly across documents, regardless of doc type.
60 NDA / 20 MSA / 18 invoice / 2 amendment reviews — proportional to volume.
25 reviews per doc type — equal allocation regardless of risk or volume.
An allocation that over-samples high-risk strata (e.g., 25 NDA / 25 MSA / 20 invoice / 30 amendment) so each stratum has enough reviews to detect a regression.
explanations: Uniform sampling is the structure stratification corrects; this isn't stratified.
Volume-proportional allocation is uniform sampling on the count side and leaves the amendment stratum at 2 reviews/day — under-powered.
Equal-per-stratum can be a defensible heuristic but isn't 'stratified random sampling' in the statistical sense unless tied to risk; the canonical answer is risk-weighted.
Correct — stratified random sampling allocates budget across strata so each stratum gets statistical power, deliberately over-sampling rare/high-risk segments.

question: A team notices their auto-ship rate is 84%, with 16% routed to human review. Leadership asks if they should tune the calibration to 'auto-ship 95% to cut review costs.' What's the principled response?
options: Raise the calibrated-confidence thresholds globally to push more cases above the auto-ship bar.
Auto-ship rate is an output of the routing rule, not a target — pushing it up by relaxing thresholds will auto-ship more wrong extractions.
Switch from calibrated to raw confidence; raw is more permissive.
Disable contradiction routing to free up the cases it currently sends to review.
explanations: Raising thresholds globally pushes risky segments into auto-ship; the right unit of decision is per-cell, not global.
Correct — auto-ship volume is a consequence of the rule. Tuning the rule to hit a target auto-ship rate inverts the logic and ships more errors.
Raw confidence is uncalibrated; switching to it for permissiveness re-introduces exactly the failure mode calibration solved.
Contradiction routing exists because confidence alone misses cross-field inconsistency; disabling it ships known-broken extractions.

question: A team writes: 'Aggregate accuracy is 98.2% on the validation set. We propose auto-shipping all extractions with raw model confidence ≥ 0.9.' List the failures in this sentence.
options: It uses an aggregate, it routes on raw (uncalibrated) confidence, and it doesn't validate per (doc type, field) cell.
It uses 98.2% instead of 99% as the bar; everything else is sound.
It uses raw confidence; the aggregate and per-cell concerns are not real failures.
Nothing is wrong; this is the standard automation pattern.
explanations: Correct — three independent failures: aggregate-not-segment, raw-not-calibrated confidence, and missing per-cell validation. All three are tested in this topic.
The threshold magnitude isn't the issue; the structural issues are aggregate masking, uncalibrated confidence, and absent per-cell validation.
All three are real and independent failures the topic warns against.
This is the canonical wrong pattern the topic exists to flag.

question: An extraction system reports calibrated confidence 0.97 on a field — calibration was performed on data that's 6 months old. Production has since shifted to a new vendor template. What concern does this raise?
options: Calibration ages: distribution shift breaks the calibration map, so 0.97 calibrated may no longer correspond to 97% real accuracy on the new templates.
Calibration is permanent once computed; this is fine.
Confidence scores degrade over time independent of input distribution.
The model's training data is stale; calibration is unaffected.
explanations: Correct — calibration is computed on a labelled set; if the population shifts, the map can decouple from reality, which is the drift problem ongoing stratified sampling exists to detect.
Calibration is empirical on a snapshot; nothing about it is permanent across distribution shifts.
Confidence scores don't 'age' on their own — what ages is the relationship between the score and accuracy when inputs shift.
Foundation-model training is unrelated; the issue is the input distribution shifting away from the calibration set.

question: An auto-ship pipeline relies on calibrated confidence ≥ 0.97 per cell, with no contradiction check. The downstream system flags an integrity bug: extracted line items don't sum to the extracted total in 2% of auto-shipped invoices. What's the minimal correct architectural fix?
options: Raise the per-cell calibrated-confidence threshold to 0.99.
Add internal-contradiction routing: extractions whose fields fail to reconcile go to human review regardless of confidence.
Drop calibration entirely and re-route everything to humans.
Replace the calibrated confidence with raw confidence to widen the review queue.
explanations: Raising the threshold doesn't catch high-confidence-but-self-inconsistent extractions; that's the gap contradictions fill.
Correct — contradictions are the second routing signal precisely for this failure mode; the OR-rule (low confidence OR contradiction) closes the gap.
Reverting to full human review defeats the automation goal; adding contradiction routing is the targeted fix.
Raw confidence is uncalibrated; switching to it is a regression, not a fix.

question: A team reports: 'We sample 1% uniformly for review and our error rate is 1.2%.' Which segment-specific error rates is this number actually evidence about?
options: All segments equally; uniform sampling guarantees per-segment estimates.
Only the dominant segments; rare segments are nearly absent from the sample, so their error rates are essentially unmeasured.
Only the rare segments; uniform sampling oversamples rare events.
None — uniform sampling cannot estimate any error rate.
explanations: Uniform sampling gives an aggregate estimate; per-segment estimates require enough sample in each segment, which uniform sampling doesn't guarantee.
Correct — the 1.2% is a volume-weighted aggregate; rare segments contribute almost no data points, so their per-segment error rates are statistically uninformed.
Uniform sampling under-samples rare events relative to risk; it doesn't oversample them.
Uniform sampling can estimate the aggregate; the failure is that the aggregate masks segments.

question: A reviewer challenges: 'If we calibrate per (doc type, field), don't we overfit to the validation set?' What's the right framing?
options: Yes — per-cell calibration is overfitting; only global calibration is statistically sound.
Calibration is by definition empirical on a held-out labelled set; overfitting is mitigated by adequate per-cell sample size, not by collapsing the granularity.
Per-cell calibration is fine but only on the training set, not on validation.
Validation sets cannot be used for calibration; only production data can.
explanations: Global calibration is what under-fits — it averages over heterogeneous segments. Granularity is the right axis; sample size per cell is the variance concern.
Correct — calibration needs enough labelled data per cell; the answer to thin cells is more labels, not coarser calibration that re-introduces aggregate masking.
Calibration is computed on a held-out validation set, never on the training set used to fit the model — that would be a fundamental statistical error.
Production data is unlabelled by definition; you can't calibrate without ground truth, which is what a labelled validation set provides.

question: An extraction returns: line_item_total 0.99 calibrated, footer_total 0.99 calibrated, but line_item_total = $1,200 and footer_total = $1,250. A junior engineer says 'Both fields are at 0.99, ship them.' What's the precise error in their reasoning?
options: 0.99 is too low a threshold; they should require 0.999.
0.99 calibrated confidence is impossible in a real system.
Per-field calibration is independent of cross-field consistency — two correctly-calibrated 0.99 fields can still encode a contradictory document, which is exactly what contradiction routing catches.
Confidence scores must agree exactly across reconcilable fields, and 0.99 vs 0.99 doesn't agree.
explanations: Threshold magnitude is unrelated; the issue is that confidence and contradictions are independent signals.
0.99 calibrated confidence is achievable on well-calibrated cells; impossibility isn't the issue.
Correct — calibration speaks to per-field accuracy probabilities; it does not entail mutual consistency, which requires the contradiction check.
Confidence scores aren't required to numerically agree — they're per-field probabilities. The contradiction is between the extracted values, not the scores.

question: Which of these production stories is the most accurate description of what 'aggregate accuracy hides segment failure' looks like in practice?
options: A pipeline at 99.5% aggregate accuracy has uniform per-cell accuracy at 99–99.7%; everything is fine.
A pipeline at 96.9% aggregate accuracy has 95% of volume in clean PDFs at 99% accuracy and 5% of volume in scanned faxes at 60% accuracy — the scanned-fax segment is the silent risk.
A pipeline at 50% aggregate accuracy has uniform 50% per-cell accuracy; the model is broken everywhere.
A pipeline at 80% aggregate accuracy has uniform 80% per-cell accuracy; no segment is masked.
explanations: Uniform per-cell accuracy means no masking is occurring; this isn't an example of the failure mode.
Correct — high aggregate plus a small, hard, low-accuracy segment is the textbook masking pattern; the headline number rounds up while a real segment runs at 60%.
Uniform 50% accuracy is just uniformly bad performance; nothing is being masked.
Uniform 80% means there's no masking — every segment matches the aggregate.

question: A team wants to express the routing rule formally. Which is correct?
options: auto_ship if (calibrated_confidence ≥ threshold) OR (no internal contradictions).
auto_ship if (raw_confidence ≥ threshold) AND (no internal contradictions).
auto_ship if (calibrated_confidence ≥ threshold) AND (no internal contradictions).
auto_ship if (calibrated_confidence ≥ threshold), regardless of contradictions.
explanations: OR makes the auto-ship gate weaker (any one clean signal would auto-ship); the production rule is AND on the auto-ship side.
Raw confidence is uncalibrated; routing on it re-introduces the calibration failure mode the rule is meant to prevent.
Correct — both signals must be clean: high calibrated confidence AND no contradictions; the queue gets the complement (low confidence OR contradiction).
Ignoring contradictions misses the failure mode where each field is high-confidence but the document disagrees with itself.

question: A pipeline reports 99.1% aggregate accuracy, with the worst per-cell at 98.5%. The team proposes turning off all human review. What's the best response?
options: Turn off all human review — every per-cell is above any reasonable bar.
Turn off review for cells above the per-cell bar, but keep an ongoing stratified sample running to detect drift.
Keep full human review on every extraction indefinitely; automation is too risky.
Turn off review only for the highest-volume cell.
explanations: Eliminating review entirely loses your drift signal; production populations shift, and you'll learn about regressions only from downstream complaints.
Correct — automate cells that pass per-cell bars, but keep a stratified review sample so drift surfaces early; this is the steady-state production pattern.
Full review forever defeats the automation goal in a pipeline whose per-cell accuracy passes the bar; the right move is automate-plus-monitor.
Cherry-picking by volume re-introduces aggregate-style thinking; the per-cell bar is the right gate, plus drift monitoring.

question: Why are aggregate metrics 'mathematically' biased toward the dominant segment, in a way that segment-level metrics aren't?
options: Because the aggregate is a volume-weighted average; the dominant segment's value pulls the aggregate toward itself, while a small low-accuracy segment's contribution is multiplied by its small weight.
Because aggregate accuracy uses a logarithm that exponentially down-weights rare segments.
Because the model fundamentally favours common document types in its outputs.
Because validation sets always over-represent rare documents, distorting the aggregate.
explanations: Correct — this is the arithmetic of weighted averages: an aggregate of 95%×99% + 5%×60% rounds up to 96.95%, hiding the 60% segment in the small weight.
There is no logarithm; the masking is straightforward weighted averaging.
Model behaviour isn't the cause of metric masking; the metric arithmetic is.
Validation sets typically reflect production distribution; the masking happens regardless of how the validation set is composed.

question: A reviewer asks: 'If raw model confidence is unreliable, why bother having the model output it at all?' What's the right answer?
options: Raw confidence is the input to calibration; without it there's nothing to calibrate, and calibrated confidence drives routing.
Raw confidence is purely decorative and serves no purpose.
Raw confidence is used directly for billing and pricing.
Raw confidence is needed for fine-tuning the model.
explanations: Correct — raw confidence is the substrate calibration is built on; you need a per-extraction signal to bucket on, and calibration produces the actually-trustworthy probability from it.
It isn't decorative when used as the input to a calibration pipeline; it's decorative only if used directly as a routing threshold.
Pricing and billing are out of scope and unrelated to calibration.
Fine-tuning is out of scope; calibration is the in-scope use of raw confidence.

question: A confused engineer says: 'We're using stratified random sampling — we sample 1% of every doc type uniformly within that doc type.' What's the subtle issue?
options: Sampling 1% per doc type is mathematically impossible.
Sampling 1% per doc type is correctly stratified and there's no issue.
Stratified sampling requires sampling exactly 0.5% per stratum.
Sampling 1% per doc type still under-samples a 200-doc rare segment (only 2 reviews/day) — the budget needs to be allocated by risk, not by uniform percentage.
explanations: It is mathematically possible; the issue is statistical power on rare strata.
Equal-percentage stratification is uniform sampling rebadged; it doesn't fix the rare-segment under-sampling problem.
There's no canonical percentage; stratification allocates budget by risk to give each stratum statistical power.
Correct — uniform percentage per stratum still leaves rare strata under-powered; stratification's value comes from over-sampling high-risk/rare segments, not from equal percentages.

question: A team trains a downstream classifier to flag extractions for human review and replaces calibrated-confidence routing with classifier output. What's the most important pre-deployment check this topic emphasises?
options: That the classifier's outputs are themselves validated per (document type, field) cell — otherwise you've just moved the segment-masking problem to a new model.
That the classifier uses the same model architecture as the extraction model.
That the classifier runs faster than calibrated-confidence routing.
That the classifier produces scores between 0 and 1.
explanations: Correct — any routing signal, whether confidence-based or classifier-based, must be validated per cell; segment-level evaluation is the underlying principle, and a classifier doesn't exempt you from it.
Architecture matching is not the principle; per-cell validation is.
Latency isn't the criterion the topic emphasises; segment-level validation is.
Output range is a numeric detail; per-cell validation is the substantive check.

question: A confident-sounding stakeholder claims: 'Our model says 95% confidence on this extraction, so the extraction is 95% likely to be correct.' Under what conditions is this claim actually true?
options: It's true by definition for any modern LLM.
It's true only when 95% raw confidence has been empirically calibrated — on a labelled validation set, on this specific (doc type, field) cell — to ~95% real accuracy.
It's true whenever the extraction passes a JSON-schema check.
It's never true; confidence and accuracy are unrelated.
explanations: Modern LLMs are not calibrated by default; raw confidence often diverges sharply from real accuracy on hard segments.
Correct — the claim is sound only on a calibrated, segment-specific basis. Without that, '95%' is a self-report, not a probability.
JSON-schema validation checks structure, not content correctness, and has no bearing on the calibration of confidence.
Confidence and accuracy are correlated and become statistically meaningful once calibrated; 'never true' is too strong.

question: A team deploys with full per-cell validation and per-cell calibrated thresholds, and runs a stratified review sample. After 4 weeks, no per-cell metric has drifted. Leadership asks: 'Can we reduce the stratified sample size since accuracy is stable?' What's the principled trade-off?
options: Yes — stable accuracy means the sample is no longer needed.
Reducing sample size reduces the statistical power to detect future regressions; the trade-off is review-cost vs early-detection latency, and is a budget choice, not a metric choice.
No — sample size is fixed by regulation and cannot be reduced.
No — sample size must always equal 100% of incoming volume to be meaningful.
explanations: Stability now doesn't mean stability forever; the sample exists to catch regressions early.
Correct — reducing the sample raises the latency to detect a regression, so it's a cost-vs-detection-latency trade-off teams make explicitly, segment by segment.
There's no general regulation governing sample size; this is a design decision driven by risk.
100% review is full human review, the opposite of automation; the sample exists precisely so review is partial.

question: Which combination of practices, taken together, defines the production-grade extraction-review architecture this topic prescribes?
options: Aggregate validation; raw confidence routing; ad-hoc human review on user complaints.
Per-cell validation; raw confidence routing; uniform random sampling for monitoring.
Aggregate validation; calibrated confidence routing; no ongoing review post-deployment.
Per-cell validation before automating; per-cell calibrated confidence thresholds; routing on calibrated confidence OR contradictions; ongoing stratified review for drift.
explanations: Three failure modes — aggregate masking, uncalibrated routing, complaint-driven review (no proactive sampling).
Mixes a correct piece (per-cell validation) with two wrong ones (raw confidence, uniform sampling).
Mixes a wrong piece (aggregate validation) and missing ongoing review with a correct one (calibrated routing); leaves drift undetected.

Correct — this is the full prescription: segment-level validation, calibrated per-cell thresholds, OR-routing on confidence and contradictions, and stratified ongoing monitoring. Each piece protects the others.
